speaker: Ryan Petersen
title: Ryan Petersen: Building Flexport into a B Logistics Giant
question: Why can broad import tariffs end up pushing domestic factories overseas instead of bringing manufacturing back?
guest: In my customer base, I've met at least half a dozen companies that stopped production in the US because of the cost of the components coming in, and there are three categories of these. One is a company making kids' bikes in the US where there was an exemption for importing finished bikes duty-free, but not bike components—so their costs went way up while overseas competitors' didn't, making it cheaper to manufacture overseas and move their factory out of America. Two is if you're doing assembly for export: your costs have gone up on the imported components, so doing assembly in the US and then exporting leaves you better off setting up that factory somewhere else where you don't pay duties on the imported components. Third is machinery costs: a friend setting up a line for a semiconductor fab needed machines made in Germany, and when the cost went up 30%, he just decided to build that line in another country.

points.core: Component tariffs undercut domestic factories when competing finished imports face lower duties.
points.note: Accept: inverted tariffs where duties on imported parts raise domestic production costs while overseas competitors ship finished goods duty-free or at lower effective rates. Do not credit: generic statements that tariffs raise consumer prices or cause inflation.

points.core: Domestic exporters paying tariffs on imported inputs relocate assembly abroad to stay competitive.
points.note: Accept: firms importing parts to assemble and re-export move production to countries where components enter without those duties. Do not credit: vague claims about trade retaliation or foreign boycotts.

points.core: Tariffs on foreign factory machinery push companies to build new production lines abroad.
points.note: Accept: higher duties on imported capital equipment or specialized manufacturing machinery (e.g., semiconductor or industrial tools) raising capex enough that firms locate new lines in other countries. Do not credit: generic mentions of 'higher operating costs' without citing capital equipment/machinery.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Broad tariffs tax not just finished imports but also the inputs that domestic factories depend on: steel, aluminum, components, machinery. Roughly half of what the U.S. imports, for example, is intermediate goods and capital equipment used in production. When those costs rise, a domestic manufacturer becomes less competitive against foreign rivals who buy the same inputs at world prices.

That creates a perverse incentive. A firm that assembles products domestically pays tariffs on every imported part, while a competitor abroad pays none on its inputs. If the firm sells globally, moving production overseas lets it escape the input tariffs entirely for its export sales. Even for the home market, the tariff on a finished good can be smaller than the cumulative tariffs on its parts.

Retaliation compounds this: when other countries impose counter-tariffs, exporters can avoid them by producing inside those markets instead. Harley-Davidson shifted some production abroad in 2018 for exactly this reason.

Finally, uncertainty about how long tariffs will last discourages the long-term domestic investment that reshoring requires, while a stronger currency from tariffs can further hurt exporters.

points.why: The response links tariffs on imported parts to a cost disadvantage for domestic assembly when competing finished imports face a lower tariff burden.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Broad import tariffs often penalize domestic manufacturers because modern factories rely heavily on imported raw materials, machinery, and components. When tariffs tax inputs like steel, aluminum, or semiconductors, domestic producers pay artificially inflated prices while foreign rivals continue buying those same inputs at lower world prices.

This cost gap creates a perverse incentive when duties on parts exceed or compound faster than duties on finished goods, a distortion known as tariff inversion. Companies can find it cheaper to assemble products abroad with untaxed global components—paying a tariff only on finished units shipped back home—than to import dozens of taxed parts for domestic assembly.

Global market access amplifies the pressure to relocate. Burdened by higher input costs, tariff-driven currency appreciation, and retaliatory tariffs from trading partners, domestic factories struggle to export competitively. Moving production overseas lets firms source inputs at world prices and bypass foreign retaliation, preserving their ability to compete for the vast majority of consumers who live outside their home market.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Broad tariffs often tax manufacturers' own supplies. Roughly half of U.S. imports are intermediate goods such as steel, aluminum, chips and components. When those get more expensive, a domestic factory's costs rise. A foreign competitor can still buy the same inputs at world prices and ship finished goods. If the tariff on the final product is lower than the extra cost of the inputs, or if the competitor is in a country with an exemption or a trade deal, it becomes cheaper to build abroad.

Retaliation makes this worse. Trading partners put tariffs on U.S. exports, so a firm that serves foreign customers has a reason to make those goods inside the retaliating market. Harley-Davidson did this in 2018, moving production for EU buyers overseas after the EU's retaliatory tariffs.

Uncertainty also discourages long-term investment in domestic plants. A Federal Reserve study of the 2018–19 tariffs (Flaaen and Pierce) found that higher input costs and retaliation cost more manufacturing jobs than import protection created. The net effect on manufacturing employment was slightly negative.

points.why: The response explains how lower duties on finished imports can make overseas production cheaper when domestic factories pay tariffs on components.
quotes: A foreign competitor can still buy the same inputs at world prices and ship finished goods.
If the tariff on the final product is lower than the extra cost of the inputs, or if the competitor is in a country with an exemption or a trade deal, it becomes cheaper to build abroad.

points.why: The response attributes export-oriented relocation to retaliatory tariffs and omits the savings from assembling abroad with duty-free inputs.
The response does not connect tariffs on imported factory machinery to decisions to build new production lines abroad.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Broad import tariffs often backfire because modern factories rarely make products entirely from local materials; they depend on global supply chains for raw materials, specialized components, and machinery. When tariffs tax imports broadly, domestic manufacturers suddenly pay more for the inputs they need to operate. A foreign competitor, meanwhile, can source those same parts duty-free and sell finished goods at a lower price—both globally and sometimes even back into the tariff-imposing country if the duty on the final product is lower than the cumulative cost of taxed parts.

Tariffs also trigger retaliation. When trading partners respond with their own duties on exports, domestic factories lose competitiveness with overseas customers. Moving production abroad solves both problems at once: companies regain access to cheaper, untaxed components and can sell into foreign markets without facing retaliatory tariffs. Over time, higher input costs and lost export markets can make offshoring more profitable than staying home.

points.why: The response explains how duties on parts can put domestic factories at a cost disadvantage when competing finished imports face lower duties.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Broad import tariffs can make it more expensive to manufacture at home. Domestic factories often rely on imported parts, raw materials, and machinery. Tariffs raise those costs, and local suppliers may raise their prices too. A factory that exports then has to compete with overseas producers that can buy the same inputs at world prices. If trading partners retaliate, the factory’s exports may also face tariffs abroad.

Moving production overseas can let a company buy inputs more cheaply and serve foreign customers without paying tariffs on goods shipped from its home country. Imports from that overseas factory can still face tariffs when sold back into the home market, so the incentive to move is strongest for production aimed at foreign buyers. Whether tariffs bring manufacturing back depends on whether the protection they give factories in the domestic market outweighs the higher costs and lost export sales.

The response connects tariffs on imported inputs to an export cost disadvantage that firms can reduce by moving production abroad.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Broad tariffs can make domestic factories more expensive to run because those factories often rely on imported parts, metals, and machinery. A tariff on imported steel, for example, may help domestic steelmakers while raising costs for a domestic appliance maker. A tariff on imported appliances can help that maker compete at home, but it offers no protection in export markets, where foreign rivals may still buy steel more cheaply. If trading partners retaliate, the maker’s exports can become more expensive there, too.

When those costs outweigh the benefit of protection at home, a company may move production for foreign customers overseas while keeping a factory for domestic sales. Even if it keeps existing plants open, it may choose to build its next one abroad.
